prompt.en: A resistor in a single series string breaks internally. What happens to current in the other resistors?

text.en: It stops throughout the string because the only path is broken.

feedback.en: Every series part is in the same path. An open part stops current in that path.

text.en: Only the broken part loses current; the others keep their original current.

feedback.en: That describes separate paths. This series string has only one path.

text.en: It rises because one resistance has been removed.

feedback.en: An open is not a jumper replacing the part. It breaks the path instead.

text.en: It divides among the remaining resistors.

feedback.en: The remaining resistors have no parallel branches for current to divide through.

explanation.en: Topology matters: a series break opens the whole loop.

prompt.en: A supply holds its voltage steady while a second equal resistor branch is added in parallel. How do the original branch current and total current change?

feedback.en: The original current stays unchanged, but the new branch adds its own current to the total.

text.en: The original branch current halves; total current stays unchanged.

feedback.en: The supply holds the same voltage across each branch, so the original resistor still draws the same current.

text.en: The original branch current stays unchanged; total current doubles.

feedback.en: Each equal branch sees the full supply voltage and draws the original branch current.

text.en: The original branch current doubles; total current doubles.

feedback.en: Only the total doubles. The original branch has unchanged resistance and voltage.

explanation.en: Adding a parallel path changes total resistance without changing the voltage of an ideal regulated supply.

prompt.en: Four equal-resistance branches share power evenly. One resistor is rated 1 W and the other three are rated 3 W each. Which total power ceiling follows before practical margin?

text.en: 10 W, by adding every nameplate rating.

feedback.en: That total would put 2.5 W in each equal branch and overload the 1 W part.

text.en: 4 W, because each branch reaches 1 W when the lowest-rated resistor reaches its limit.

feedback.en: Equal sharing limits every branch to the weakest part's 1 W ceiling: 4 x 1 W = 4 W total.

text.en: 12 W, by applying the largest part rating to all four branches.

feedback.en: That would put 3 W in the 1 W branch. Other branches cannot lend it their unused heat rating.

text.en: 3 W, because the largest individual nameplate is the whole network's rating.

feedback.en: The largest single rating does not set the network ceiling. At 3 W total, every branch is only at 0.75 W.

explanation.en: Use each branch's actual dissipation and rating. Summing unlike wattage labels can overstate a network's safe capability.
